compression.title: Problematic Paper Screener
compression.lede: is an online platform, run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, that screens the scientific literature for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, pairing machine detection with human assessment (MMRS record; arXiv:2210.04895).

sentences.text: The Problematic Paper Screener (PPS) is an online platform, in its makers' paper, that combines automatic machine detection with human assessment to identify and flag already published problematic articles (arXiv:2210.04895); its own page says it screens the scientific literature for papers (partly) generated with tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen, and the MMRS record has it run by Guillaume Cabanac with Cyril Labbé and Alexander Magazinov since 27 February 2021, scanning the literature weekly for papers generated or disguised by tools and for references to retracted work, at the address dbrech.irit.fr.

Its unit, in the MMRS record, is a published paper flagged by a detector; CCSD, announcing Episciences' adoption, describes what it provides as a database of over one million references identified as containing problematic elements, typed by severity from articles written entirely by AI to valid articles whose references carry anomalies ("Feet of clay").

The page dates the screener "Est. February 27th, 2021" and gives its reference as Cabanac, Labbé and Magazinov (2022), presented at WCRI 2022, the 7th World Conference on Research Integrity; the paper was submitted to arXiv on 7 October 2022 by those three authors, and the MMRS record gives the same three as operator and the same founding date.

Writing in The Conversation (29 January 2025) as "a pair of computer scientists at Université de Toulouse and Université Grenoble Alpes" who specialize in detecting bogus publications, Cabanac and Labbé say that Cabanac built the automated tool, and their disclosure names him its administrator: "a public platform that uses metadata from Digital Science and PubPeer via no-cost agreements".
The page says it was "Featured in the Nature's 10 list of 2021"; The Conversation says it "was named one of 10 key developments in science by the journal Nature in 2021".

The MMRS record calls it a set of detectors run over the literature: tortured phrases, SCIgen and Mathgen papers, references annulled or under concern, and others; the page's menu, updated 2026-10-28, lists ten (Annulled, Concerning, Feet of Clay, Tortured, Suspect, SCIgen, Mathgen, Citejacked, Seek&Blastn, Problematic Cell Lines), and The Conversation, in January 2025, counted eight beside tortured phrases, among them ChatGPT fingerprints, "snippets of telltale text left behind by the AI agent".

Tortured phrases are, in the makers' article, nonsensical word sequences found "littered throughout reputable scientific journals", which "typically result from using paraphrasing tools to evade plagiarism-detection software": "the Joined Together States" for the United States, the record's example too; the screener's page quotes Nature's post of 8 August 2021: "Why say 'colossal information' instead of big data? Or 'counterfeit consciousness' instead of artificial intelligence?"

Its bibliographic detectors screen the articles citing retracted references, references marked with expressions of concern and references the screener's own detectors flag (its page), the one that finds articles citing retracted works named "Feet of Clay" (The Conversation); for a research question the MMRS record codes it as recording attribution partly, since references to retracted or concerning works are flagged.

It harvests the APIs of Crossref, "now including the Retraction Watch Database", Dimensions, PubMed and PubPeer (its page), the sources and intake the MMRS record states with the screener's page as basis.

It trawls "130 million scholarly papers every week" for signs of paper-mill production (The Conversation's standfirst, the article saying the same of Cabanac's tool), the weekly scan of 130 million publications the MMRS record gives as its cadence.

Its makers start from the claim that post-publication assessment "remains necessary to check erroneous or fraudulent scientific publications" and present the screener as "a new effective tool to curate the scientific literature" (arXiv:2210.04895); Research Signals describes it as an academic project led by Cabanac and collaborators that "combines automatic machine detection and human evaluation".
"Problematic papers are reported on PubPeer" (its page).

By The Conversation's count it had found nearly 19,000 papers with at least five tortured phrases each, more than 280 SCIgen papers, more than 764,000 articles citing retracted works (about 5,000 with five or more), and more than 70 papers carrying ChatGPT fingerprints such as "Regenerate Response"; the MMRS record carries the same figures, dated "The Conversation, 31 January 2025", where the article at theconversation.com is dated 29 January 2025.

Its makers state the limit of the fingerprint count themselves: those papers are "the tip of the tip of the iceberg", output "copy-pasted wholesale into papers without any editing (or even reading)", and "The challenge is to identify cases where chatbots are used not just for language-editing purposes but to generate content – essentially fabricating data."

The MMRS record extends that limit to the whole instrument: "A detector finds what leaves a fingerprint", and "Text machine-written cleanly, or cited sources that exist but say something else, pass beneath it."

The archive's The Evaluator Exists (#741, 19 May 2026) reads the class the screener works on, paper-mill output, as proxy gaming at industrial scale, "thousands of fraudulent publications that enter the citation network and accumulate proxy signals indistinguishable from legitimate scholarship", holds that under the proxy regime "gaming is hard to detect because the signals being gamed are themselves opaque", and sets against it an evaluator that synthetic scholarship must get past by reading, with "empirical claims that survive a citation audit".

Several publishers use it, by its makers' account, some inside the editorial workflow to spot suspect papers upfront, and it "has been instrumental in more than 1,000 retractions"; analytics companies have used it to pick out suspect authors among highly cited researchers, Cabanac has offered pro bono consulting on detection tools to actors including ClearSkies, Morressier, River Valley, Signals and STM (The Conversation), and the MMRS record says it has contributed to more than 1,000 retractions.

On 20 June 2024 Research Signals integrated the articles it flags into the Signals Graph as a new signal, "over 12,000 problematic publications that have not been retracted", cited more than 160,000 times, to give sleuths, publishers and researchers visibility of them.

On 3 July 2026 CCSD announced that Episciences analyses citations extracted from articles against the PPS database, at submission and after publication, displaying problematic citations for correction or information; of nearly 170,000 references in a first extraction, 226 were indexed in the PPS, most in the Feet of clay category.

The same announcement describes the screener as a tool to identify and filter out articles "containing methodological errors, plagiarism, data manipulation, or conflicts of interest", a description that stands beside the screener's own list of detectors.

The MMRS record files it as a monitor and calls it "the scholarly record's automated immune response", the neighbour of Academ-AI, "which reads by phrase where the screener reads by detector"; with the screener, its Academ-AI record says, that database records "machine composition entering the scholarly record unattributed: the machine is the uncredited author, and the publisher is where the reception happens."

The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle (active) apart from the observation (read, 2026-10-28); it read the screener's page for detectors, sources and start date, leaves the licence unchecked, and relates the capture of 2026-10-29 as the composition layer's account of the entity; the page itself was last updated on 2026-10-28 at 15:54.

Google's AI Overview at the name, signed out, 2026-10-29, gave the three makers, the sources and the detectors as the IRIT page and the record give them, and composed the screener at its makers' grain, with its human review stage stated and its uptake by publishers' infrastructure added (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29, checked against the MMRS record and the entity's own pages); no card cited the record, which was published the same night.

The Capture Registry records the Overview's example of a tortured phrase, "counterfeit consciousness" for artificial intelligence, as the composition's, the record's being "Joined Together States", not checked against the screener's list; the example stands on the screener's own page, in Nature's post of 8 August 2021.

The adoptions the Overview carried, Episciences and the Signals Graph, are uptake the MMRS record lacked (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29); the rail's sixth card is Crossref's video "Exploring Retraction Watch Data in Crossref 2025-05-09", admitted by its title.
